group.passage: High in the mountains of the northern Philippines, between about 800 and 1,500 meters above sea level, rice fields climb the steep slopes like a giant staircase. These are the Ifugao rice terraces, built and cared for by the Ifugao people. Today they are both a World Heritage site and, since 2011, one of the farming systems honored by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization. The terraces work as a carefully balanced whole. Above the fields stand small private forests called muyong, which families pass down from one generation to the next. These woodlots catch rainwater and slowly release it, along with nutrients, to the terraces below, keeping the fields under water all year round. Rice is harvested only once a year, yet the terraces are never idle: after the harvest, farmers grow vegetables on small piles of soil and raise fish in holes dug inside the fields. The best-known local rice, tinawon, takes its name from this yearly cycle, since the word means “once a year.” How old the terraces are is still debated. They are often said to be 2,000 years old. However, a research project led by archaeologists from the University of California, Los Angeles, has found evidence that wet-rice farming spread quickly in the highlands only after Spanish colonizers arrived around 1600. If they are right, the terraces were in part a local response to colonial pressure, showing that the Ifugao were far from passive in the face of foreign rule. Whatever their age, the terraces now face a lack of hands. Seeing little money in farming, many young Ifugao have left for jobs in the cities, leaving aging parents to repair walls and clear canals. Damage caused by natural disasters is sometimes left unrepaired, and earthworms digging into the walls can make them collapse. Some families have turned their fields into vegetable farms or given them up altogether. Those who stay are looking for ways to make the terraces pay. Tinawon, a sweet-smelling rice grown in only three places in the world, can sell for a high price. Some farmers also earn extra money by guiding visitors through the fields, letting them stay overnight, serving local rice dishes, and even inviting them to help with planting.

3.explanation_zh: they 所在句是「如果 they 是對的」，「對不對」只能用來說提出看法或證據的人。前一句的主詞是 a research project（單數），由 archaeologists 帶領，找到「濕地稻作在西班牙人約 1600 年到來後才迅速擴散」的證據。所以 they 指的是這些考古學家，答案是 C。

evidence: Seeing little money in farming, many young Ifugao have left for jobs in the cities, leaving aging parents to repair walls and clear canals.

如果原因被解決了，可能會有什麼結果？

translation_zh.text:
在菲律賓北部的山區，海拔大約 800 到 1,500 公尺之間，稻田像一座巨大的階梯般爬上陡峭的山坡。這就是伊富高梯田，由伊富高人建造並照顧。如今它既是世界遺產，也從 2011 年起被聯合國糧食及農業組織列為表揚的農業系統之一。

梯田是一個經過精心平衡的整體。田地上方有被稱為 muyong 的小片私有林，由各家族一代傳一代。這些林地會留住雨水，再慢慢把水連同養分釋放到下方的梯田，讓田地一年到頭都浸在水裡。稻子一年只收成一次，但梯田從不閒置：收割後，農民在一小堆一小堆的土上種菜，並在田裡挖的小洞養魚。當地最有名的稻米 tinawon 就是以這種一年一次的循環命名，因為這個字的意思是「一年一次」。

梯田有多古老，至今仍有爭議。人們常說梯田已有 2,000 年歷史。然而，一個由美國加州大學洛杉磯分校考古學家帶領的研究計畫找到證據，顯示濕地稻作是在西班牙殖民者約 1600 年到來之後，才在這片高地迅速擴散。如果他們是對的，梯田在某種程度上是對殖民壓力的在地回應，顯示伊富高人面對外來統治時一點也不被動。

不論梯田有多古老，它們現在都面臨人手不足的問題。許多年輕的伊富高人覺得務農賺不到錢，紛紛到城市工作，留下年邁的父母修補田埂、清理水道。天災造成的損壞有時無人修復，鑽進田埂的蚯蚓也可能讓田埂崩塌。有些家庭把田地改成菜園，或乾脆放棄不耕種了。

留下來的人正設法讓梯田能夠賺錢。tinawon 是一種香氣濃郁、全世界只有三個地方種植的稻米，可以賣到好價錢。有些農民還靠著帶遊客參觀梯田來多賺一些錢：讓遊客留宿、請他們品嘗當地的米飯料理，甚至邀請他們一起插秧。
